**February 20, 1952 — a Wednesday**

You arrived in the second week of a new Elizabethan age, though the world didn't quite know it yet. Fourteen days before your birth, on February 6, King George VI died quietly in his sleep at Sandringham. His daughter Elizabeth — then 25, on a royal tour of Kenya — flew home to become Queen. The coronation was still 15 months away, and Britain was still learning to say her name on the throne. You were born into the opening hours of a reign that would last 70 years.

---

On the exact day you were born, the **1952 Oslo Winter Olympics** were in full swing — the Games ran February 14–25, and February 20 fell near their midpoint. Norway was dominant on its home snow, particularly in cross-country skiing. It was one of the last Winter Olympics before television made the Games a global spectacle; most of the world learned the results from newspapers.

---

The **Korean War** had been grinding for 19 months. Armistice negotiations at Panmunjom were stalled over the repatriation of prisoners. More than 30,000 Americans had already died. You entered a world at war, though few people called it that — the word "conflict" was preferred.

Deeper in the background was the nuclear shadow. The Soviet Union had tested its first atomic bomb in 1949. Nine months after your birth, in November 1952, the United States detonated "Ivy Mike" — the first thermonuclear device, a thousand times more powerful than Hiroshima. The Cold War arms race was not yet at its peak. You were born into its accelerating middle.

---

**Television** was in the process of swallowing American life. In 1950, roughly one in ten American homes had a set; by the end of 1952 it was closer to one in three. *I Love Lucy* had premiered just four months before you were born and was already the most-watched show in the country. You came of age in the medium's first decade, at the moment it was becoming the defining technology of the century — then lived long enough to watch it be displaced by something stranger and faster still.

---

**An exact-date coincidence, ten years on:** On February 20, 1962 — your tenth birthday — John Glenn climbed into *Friendship 7* and became the first American to orbit the Earth. Three orbits, four hours and 55 minutes. The country stopped. For a child of the Cold War, this was the moment the space race shifted. You turned ten on the day America first circled the globe from space.

---

**The world you've lived through**

The person born February 20, 1952 is 74 years old today. Consider the span: you were a teenager during the civil rights movement and the Kennedy assassination. You were 17 when Apollo 11 landed on the moon. You were in your early twenties when Watergate ended a presidency and the Vietnam War finally closed. You were 37 when the Berlin Wall came down and the Soviet empire began to dissolve — events your childhood had been told were impossible. You were 49 on September 11, 2001.

You entered the workforce before personal computers existed, watched the internet emerge from a government project into the infrastructure of everything, and carried a device in your pocket that would have seemed preposterous in the world you were born into.

The February morning in 1952 that you entered was cold in the geopolitical sense: two nuclear superpowers, a war in Korea, a young Queen on a throne, and a television set in the corner of the living room that was just learning what it could do. The colonial map of Africa was still largely intact. No human being had yet been to space. The word "software" didn't exist.

You have watched every one of those certainties dissolve. That's not a common thing to be able to say.
